text: This is Sentinel. An A I powered security app for Windows and Mac, that works completely offline.
In the next few minutes, I'll show you how it finds open ports, spots apps talking to servers they shouldn't, and fixes vulnerabilities with a single click.
Everything starts on the dashboard. One scan checks your open ports, your network connections, and your system's security settings.
On the left are the most exposed ports, ranked by risk, along with the application that opened each one.
In the middle is your overall security score. This machine scores poorly, with four critical issues.
On the right, the vulnerability board counts open issues by severity, including two that attackers are actively exploiting right now.
Below that, you can see how exposed your ports are, what Sentinel recommends doing about them, and the state of every outbound connection.
Let's look at the open ports. Each row shows the port, the service, and the exact program behind it. Its name, process I D, user, and file location.
Click any row, and Sentinel's A I explains the risk in plain English.
This one is a red flag. Port forty-four forty-four, the default port for Metasploit reverse shells, opened by a program running from a temporary folder.
To close it, click Close port. Sentinel offers to block it in the firewall, and it can also stop the program behind it.
I'll choose, Yes, close port. Windows asks for administrator permission, and the port is blocked instantly.
Blocked ports are marked with a lock, and you can undo any block with one click.
Next, the network monitor. Every fifteen seconds, Sentinel checks which applications are connecting out, and exactly where to.
Here, it caught a program called update dot exe, sending traffic to a cryptocurrency mining pool. That's a classic sign of crypto jacking.
And this file, opened from the Downloads folder, is talking to a raw I P address, on a port used by remote access trojans.
Sentinel also learns what's normal for each app. After the first day, any brand new destination is flagged as an anomaly.
For strict control, switch to Allowlist mode. Then, any destination you haven't approved is flagged as unauthorised.
One click blocks the address in the firewall. And if you don't recognise the program, Sentinel can stop it too.
Now, vulnerabilities. Sentinel audits your operating system, and checks your installed apps against a built in database of known exploits.
Findings are grouped by category, and sorted by severity. Anything being exploited in the wild is clearly marked.
Click, How to fix, and you get a full playbook. Why it matters, the manual steps, and the exact commands Sentinel will run.
Click, Apply fix automatically. Sentinel applies the fix, then re-checks the system, to confirm it's really fixed.
For missing patches, run a deep scan, and Sentinel lists every update that Windows or mac O S hasn't installed yet.
All of this feeds the A I advisor. You can ask it anything about your system.
It answers using your live scan results and its built in security knowledge. No internet, and no cloud model required.
On the right is your action plan, ordered by impact versus effort, so you always know what to fix first.
After fixing things, press Refresh, and anything that's resolved drops off the plan.
If you have a local A I model installed with Ollama, Sentinel can use it for more conversational answers. But everything works without it.
Finally, settings. Here you manage your allowed and blocked domains, and import extra threat intelligence feeds whenever you're online.
Every firewall rule Sentinel creates is listed here, so you can undo it at any time. And the activity log records every action.
And that's Sentinel. Your ports, your network, and your patches, all in one place, and completely offline.
